items.speaker: INGRID LEARY
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. First, I’d like to
thank the Minister, the Hon David Seymour, for his considerable contribution just before
the break. I appreciate his comments that he thought some of the things were out of scope,
but actually I would put it to him that this was a bit more interesting and on poin t for,
particularly, members of the public, who are interested in this issue, instead of going
through a line-by-line analysis of the legislation. So I thank him for responding in a very
sincere and genuine way to the questions that we put.
I hope that, in that spirit, he will also consider a very genuine and sincere suggestion for
an Amendment Paper which has been submitted. I’m sure the Minister has had time to read
it. And this is about saying Labour agrees with the policy on the balance of considering
public harm and the benefits that would flow from this bill. We do think it’s a good idea to
support it, for all the reasons I’ve said before, but there is one really critical area where we
feel the risks could be mitigated, and that is with appropriate sto rage. And these are the
risks to the pharmacies, the pharmacists, but also to those who work in the pharmacies, who
don’t necessarily have the same level of choice about opting into the scheme, which the
Minister has made very clear pharmacists can do.
This Amendment Paper is in the name of my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall. It,
basically, proposes to replace clause 9, page 2, lines 23 to 25, with “9 Regulation 28
amended (Custody of controlled drugs) Revoke regulation 28(4)(e).” There’s a whole
explanatory note. I don’t need to take up the committee’s time with that. What I will do,
just briefly for people following at home, is say that the context is that the current bill, in
clause 9, removes any safe storage requirement for pseudoephedrine. We understand that
pharmacists can opt into the scheme. So, in some ways, they may or may not be opting
27 Mar 2024        Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill 2539
into any of the risks that that poses for people to ram-raid their shop or burgle their shop
or their pharmacy, or whatever. But also, as I said before, this is about the staff who work
there. They don’t have that choice. They have families to feed. And so this is about
protecting them as well.
I note, in putting this amendment there on behalf of my colleague, that we had
comments from pharmacists who said they w ere constantly burgled when
pseudoephedrine was on the shelves. One of them said 12 times per year, and the select
committee did ask advice around the storage of medicines and equivalent medicines —
one could say “analogue” medicines —and we were told that, w ith this kind of quantity,
codeine was a good comparator. And codeine, in fact, does seem to be under lock and
key. So it would be appropriate, in our view, to make sure that pseudoephedrine has the
same level of safety.
This Government really needs to do everything it can to protect pharmacists and those
who work in pharmacies from the risks of the declassification. So it is with real sincerity
and an amount of pride, actually, for the work that we did as a select committee to tease
out the issues, to really understand the context, understand what the real risks were about
pseudoephedrine to the community—it’s very easy to have moral panic and hysteria. We
understand that now there seems to be a pricing reality, with meth coming over the border,
that it is unlikely people will make pseudoephedrine at home. It is unlikely that they will
go and shop around, although we are very keen that the Minister will keep an eye on that
for all the reasons named across the House. But I would like to see the Minister adopt this
Amendment Paper.
For us, that would really seal the deal on being able to give full-hearted support to this
bill instead of just the cautious enthusiasm for it. We want people to have the benefit. We
don’t want to stop people from getting pseudoephed rine because they have to go to a
doctor or have it on prescription, but we need to keep our pharmacists safe, we need to
keep their staff safe. Ram raids are still happening. This Government said they wouldn’t
happen when they got hard on crime, whatever. Ram raids are happening, and I hope the
Minister understands the responsibility he has if and when there are ram raids if he doesn’t
adopt our Amendment Paper. So I’m very keen for the Minister to adopt it.
CHLÖE SWARBRICK (Co-Leader—Green): E te Māngai, tēnā koe. Tēnā koutou
e te Whare. This is a really short piece of legislation, and the Amendment Paper in my
name is what I’d like to speak to today, but I’d just like to contextualise that Amendment
Paper within the reason that we have this amendment bill before us.
So, as I outlined in my first and my second reading speeches, within the Misuse of Drugs
Act (MODA) there is a self-fulfilling prophecy which continues to entrench an anti-health
or anti - evidence-based approach to substances as classified within MODA 1975. To that
effect, there is a requirement that if you are to introduce a new substance for classification,
and therefore to bring along with it new criminal penalties, you only need to pass an Order
in Council, which is typically rubber-stamped and waved through Parliament within a few
minutes. However, if you are to declassify or to down -classify a substance, you need an
entire amendment bill, which is the reason that we have this Misuse of Drugs
(Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill b efore us today. Obviously, the intent of this
Government is to try and get this passed before Christmas, which is the very reason that
we’ve had the deeply truncated select committee process, but what this speaks to is the fact
that there are fundamental flaws within the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975.
So that’s where I now get to, the Amendment Paper in my name. This Amendment
Paper would insert new clauses 4AA and 4AB and, effectively, would require that the
Minister institute or create or commence a review on the operation of the broader Misuse
of Drugs Act 1975. This is entirely consistent with the need for us to operate in a direction
which is an evidence-based and harm minimisation approach to substances and, I’d say,
2540                 Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
entirely aligned with the very arguments and rationale that the Minister in the chair, David
Seymour, is making when it comes to this reclassification or down -classification bill
when it comes to pseudoephedrine.
To that effect, we have seen it reflected in the Law Commission’s work from 2011;
from He Ara Oranga, the mental health and addiction inquiry; and Turuki! Turuki!, the
Safe and Effective Justice Advisory Group review—all of which, effectively, said we just
need a straight-up repeal and replacement to replace the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 with
a health-based, harm minimisation type of approach. But in lieu of having that political
consensus, why not add another review to the pile so that, hopefully, a Government
further down the track does the right thing when it comes to the evidence and a  harm
minimisation type of approach.
I guess that’s just the baseline appeal that we would like to make across the House today
as the Greens: entirely consistent with the approach that we have taken on cigarettes, on
alcohol, on cannabis, and on all other substances, including pseudoephedrine, let’s take
an evidence-based, harm minimisation approach, but let’s apply that to substances across
the board. Why not have an entire review of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, because as the
Minister is underscoring in his rationale for this legislation in front of us today, the
classification schemes and the moral panics that tend to be associated with them simply
are not working and are not fit for purpose.

items.speaker: Hon GINNY ANDERSEN
items.text: Thank you very much, Madam Chair—thank
you. Look, I’ll just take a short call. Even though it was an incredibly short time for select
committee to hear submissions and gather evidence around what the impact of this bill will
have on communities, one of the points that I thought was really interesting is that there’s
a proportion within New Zealand of people who have either complex drug and alcohol—
a range of issues, that will take whatever’s going at the moment. At the time, that once was
synthetic cannabis; other times, there’s been new kinds of drugs—fentanyl was a real risk
that we’ve seen in other countries. But one of the observations is that as pseudoephedrine
becomes more readily available, the group of frequent drug users in New Zealand will use
this drug and, potentially, use it to manufacture methamphetamine.
So I think with that power to change the law for the Government, there also comes
responsibility to talk about what types of addiction services will be made mor e readily
available to those people in our community who need that assistance but aren’t yet still
receiving it. So I would be really interested to hear from the Minister: if there is going to
be more readily available pseudoephedrine within the community, then what are the steps
that will be taken to provide communities with the support, treatment, and ways of having
more wellbeing, more supported transitions, and therapeutic communities that assist
people to make positive choices and to move away from har mful abuse of substances?
When you’re making a substance like this, which can be potentially harmful, more readily
available, it would be good to have an understanding about what the Government’s plan
is to provide assistance into those areas where they might be more harmful.
GREG O’CONNOR (Labour—Ōhāriu): Thank you, Madam Speaker. I’ve just got
some questions of the Minister; they’ll be around the context of this. Now, I accept this
is a very simple bill that by itself, out of any context, merely changes the legal status of a
substance. However, as the Minister knows, nothing ever happens in isolation, and I think
it’s important to note that the difference with methamphetamine from every other drug,
virtually, that we deal with—some of them being mentioned by my colleague previously,
Ginny Andersen—is that this starts life, as does every ingredient which goes into it: every
precursor is legal when it starts life, and it’s only when they are put together that you have
an illegal substance.
I’ll give an example of that. When I was a younger police officer, we had a major
heroin epidemic in New Zealand, and it was not unusual to have two or three heroin
27 Mar 2024        Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill 2541
overdose deaths in Wellington. Now, that was cured overnight, because the Mr Asia
syndicate —the very efficient Mr Asia syndicate —had been bringing basically all the
heroin into New Zealand. So when they were busted, they fell apart quite badly —
ended up with one of them handless and headless in a quarry in northern England. As
a result, the whole syndicate collapsed and there was no heroin in New Zealand for
quite some time.
The next lot of heroin arrived because the very resourceful criminals and drug addicts
who were left actually started to make heroin, what we called homebake heroin, using
codeine-based products—very resourceful. We hadn’t had a problem for abou t three or
four years; all of a sudden, we had a problem again, where this homebake heroin, which
actually turned out to be more of a problem than heroin itself, was actually harder on the
body and resulted in more deaths than heroin did itself.
Now, comin g forward to the question that I’m asking here: has the Minister, in
bringing forward this legislation, considered what may happen here? It was a very
unlikely scenario that a country awash with heroin all of a sudden would have no white
powder available, and the same thing could actually happen. New Zealand has relatively
secure borders, unlike most countries where you can drive into or sail into —well, you
can sail into New Zealand but you lose control of the product. It’s actually quite
conceivable in New  Zealand that we could end up with very little heroin around, as we
did during the COVID lockdowns, I might say, when it was very difficult to obtain this.
Now, with this product now available —there are other products; the main ones, things
like red phosph orus, some of the acetic acids whose names I could never quite
pronounce, let alone remember, but there was about four or five basic core ingredients
that went into this.
Has the Minister considered the importance of ensuring that there is a monitoring
regime so that by, for example, working out how much red phosphorus is being sold,
another essential ingredient —some of those other core products are actually being
sold, so if the amount of them being sold, stolen, or otherwise acquired starts to rise, is
there anything that the member has considered? Certainly, there’s nothing I can see in
the bill that will just give that security that this simple bill won’t result in us going back
to the old homebake heroin situation or allowing young amateurs around, part icularly,
school kids. Also, bearing in mind, we have a regime now where things are much more
readily available through mail order, through various sales regimes, where those other
ingredients are much easier to get hold of now. So is the Minister happy th at we’re not
actually re-establishing the conditions where we could actually end up with a problem
in the future without some sort of monitoring regime to make sure that we have that
reassurance that it won’t happen?
Hon DAVID SEYMOUR (Associate Minister of Health (Pharmac)) : Well, I just
want to acknowledge a couple of members that have risen to their feet and made speeches
or asked questions.
In Ingrid Leary’s case, an Amendment Paper that she is speaking on, on behalf of
Ayesha Verrall—the basic thrust of the Amendment Paper is that pharmacies would be
required to keep cough medicine, or pseudoephedr ine-based cough medicine, in safes.
This is something that was actually submitted on during the select committee process.
I’m advised that pharmacists have made it clear to the Ministry of Health that that is
impractical for them to do.
Secondly, I need t o make it clear to the committee that it is actually not currently a
requirement to keep pseudoephedrine medications in safes in pharmacists. So the notion
that this legislation is taking away that requirement is untrue, and not only is it untrue, it
couldn’t be true, if somebody knew that basic fact.
2542                 Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
Finally, I’ll just make the point that there’s nothing to stop a pharmacy from keeping
their pseudoephedrine-based cough and cold medicine in a safe. To legislate that they have
to do it would make their business unworkable. I don’t think that’s a responsible thing to
do. The Government does not accept that particular Amendment Paper.
We had a speech from Chlöe Swarbrick which appeared to be completely out of order,
trying to promote another policy area that is not actually a part of this debate because it
is not part of what was agreed to at the second reading.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
items.text: That’s not your job. We have someone else to do that for us.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: Somebody said it is not my job. Well, actually, reading the
Standing Orders to know what a committee stage of a debate is about—that actually is a part
of my job, and it might surprise the member to learn that it is part of his job too. If only he
opened the Standing Orders, he might be astonished what he could learn.
Finally, Greg O’Connor—and I’ve got to say, while I was listening to Greg O’Connor,
Hello Sailor’s “Blue Lady” was ringing in my ears. Greg O’Connor has got to be one of
the best recounters. What I took from his story about heroin in the 1970s being replaced
by homebake —I think what he is saying is that were the current supplies of
methamphetamine, which are more voluminous, more available, and cheaper than
anything available the last time we had pseudo ephedrine-based cough medicine in
pharmacies; were that supply to cease the way the supply of heroin ceased with the Mr
Asia syndicate was blown up, I think in the 1970s—it was before my time—then perhaps
there would be some other substitute; for example, people trying to manufacture meth
again. I think, sadly, it is unlikely that anything we’re doing right now is going to stop
that supply. It seems to be a strong supply.
Obviously, the Government is doing everything it can to stop. But were it to stop,
hypothetically, if I’m following Mr O’Connor’s analogy correctly, then, certainly, the
Government will look to stamp out any other sources of P, including anything relating
to the manufacture of it with other precursors or other manufacturing components, s uch
as—I think he talked about a chemical, red metal —you might be able to help me, but
I haven’t written clearly enough the chemical he mentioned, but —
Greg O’Connor: Red phosphorus.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: No, red phosphorus, yes. I think Mr O’Connor would know
that the police in their enforcement activities might well look for those kinds of things, but
it would be wrong for the Parliament or the Government to tell them exactly what to do,
because we just don’t direct the police in this country.
Finally, there were some comments from a member—I think it was Ginny Andersen—
who asked about support for the drug harm in the community, very similar to earlier
comments by Hūhana Lyndon, which I’d also addressed. In my response to t hose
comments, I pointed out that while I think it is very noble thing to have initiatives such
as Te Ara Oranga in the community, it is not strictly connected to this piece of legislation
we’re debating tonight. The assumed need for it suggests that this legislation will increase
the availability of methamphetamine, when all the evidence and most of the submissions
that came into the select committee told us that the opposite is true.

items.speaker: DAN BIDOIS
items.text: I move, That debate on this question now
close.
Motion agreed to.

REGULATORY SYSTEMS (EDUCATION) AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
items.text: I present a legislative statement
on the Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That legislative statement is published
under the authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

items.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
items.text: I move, That the Regulatory Systems (Education)
Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
During the consultation period, I had the privilege of being a member of the Education
and Workforce Committee and hearing the concerns of stakeholders in the public
regarding the matters of this bill. I want to start by, first and foremost, thanking all of
those who took time to make submissions on the bill. I’d also like to thank all of the other
members of the committee for their consideration of this bill, which makes some very
technical amendments to maintain the effectiveness of education regulatory systems,
including continuing the legacy of the 28th Māori Battalion as well as benefiting learners
who receive support from the Pacific Education Foundation.
The committee received nine submissions on the bill, covering a range of views and
suggestions. Some of the 28 th Māori Battalion company associations  made submissions
and provided their views on these proposals. The majority of submissions were supportive
of the changes that were proposed and suggestions from submitters have made useful
improvements to the bill. The committee proposed amendments to the  bill that mainly
refine and clarify the original provisions which were unanimously agreed to.
This bill makes changes to the Ngarimu VC and 28 th (Māori) Battalion Memorial
Scholarship Fund Act 1945 to confirm the Ngarimu VC and 28 th (Māori) Battalion
Memorial Scholarship Fund Board as the successor to the 28 th Māori Battalion
Association. This change will enable the board to authorise the use of words and emblems
2544 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
related to the 28 th Māori Battalion and the 28 th Māori Battalion Associ ation under the
Flags, Emblems, and Names Protection Act 1981.
The bill also creates a new position on the Ngarimu scholarship fund board to be held
by a person of Māori descent who has or is currently serving in the armed forces. This
proposal is intended  to preserve the legacy and mana of the 28 th Māori Battalion into
the future.
The Education and Workforce Committee recommended two changes to clarify this
proposal. First, the committee proposed, in addition to the bill, to state that this new
position is to be appointed by the Governor -General. This provides clarity on who will
be responsible for appointments to the new role. The Governor-General is the appropriate
person to make this appointment as they already appoint other individual positions on the
Ngarimu VC board. The Governor-General would decide who to appoint into the role on
advice from the Minister of Education and in accordance with the Public Service
Commission and Cabinet guidelines for appointments to boards where the Crown has an
interest. This will ensure that the appointment process is transparent and consistent with
other individual appointments to the Ngarimu VC board.
The committee also recommended a change to this proposal to clarify that the new
position should be held by a person of Māori descent who is serving or has served in the
armed forces rather than the New Zealand Defence Force more generally. The reference to
armed forces in the bill relates to the definition of “armed forces” in the Defence Act 1990,
which constitutes the navy, the army, and the air force, collectively. This change will make
sure that the position is held by someone with a military background rather than civilian
staff, to preserve the military legacy and mana of the 28th Māori Battalion.
The bill makes seve ral amendments to the Pacific Education Foundation Act 1972.
The Act governs the Pacific Education Foundation, which promotes and encourages
strong education outcomes for Pacific peoples in New Zealand. The board of the
foundation administers different kin ds of support for Pacific peoples living in New
Zealand. The changes to this bill to the Pacific education Act include amending the Act’s
membership and purpose provisions to enable the foundation to more effectively promote
and encourage the education of Aotearoa Pacific people.
One of the key amendments to the Pacific Education Foundation Act included in this
bill is to update the definition of “Pacific person” who can receive support from the
foundation. The new definition of “Aotearoa Pacific person” re fers to a person with
indigenous Pacific cultural heritage from a broader list of Pacific places compared to the
previous definition. The bill also enables the Governor-General, on the recommendation
of the Minister of Education through an Order in Council , to update this list to ensure it
reflects the diverse Pacific population of New Zealand.
The committee recommended an amendment to the bill so that it sets out the factors
the Minister of Education must take into account when making a recommendation to the
Governor-General to make changes to this list of Pacific places. These factors include the
location of the Pacific place, the population of those with indigenous cultural heritage
from the place living in New Zealand, and any other consultation with tha t Pacific
community. This change will ensure that any directions to make changes to the list of
places is appropriate and transparent.
The bill also updates the foundation’s authorised expenditure for purposes not
specifically identified in the Act, from $500 to $10,000 a year, as this amount hasn’t been
updated since 1972. The committee has recommended a minor change to the bill, which
modernises the language of this authorised expenditure provision.
The bill also makes technical amendments to two sets of regulations that impact the
education sector. The first is an amendment to the Health and Safety at Work (General
Risk and Workplace Management) Regulations 2016 so that the police vetting
27 Mar 2024 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 2545
requirements for workers at limited attendance childcare centres, s uch as malls or gym
creches, are consistent with the requirements in the Children’s Act 2014 and the
Education and Training Act 2020.
The second amendment updates the Children’s (Requirements for Safety Checks of
Children’s Workers) Regulations 2015 to inc lude reference to the Kiwi Access Card as
an acceptable form of identity, reflecting the name change of the 18+ Card. The
committee did not propose any changes to either of these amendments.
The bill makes changes that uphold the mana and the legacy of the  Ngarimu VC and
28th Māori Battalion, supports the work of the Pacific Education Foundation, and ensures
that the education regulatory systems are fit for purpose.
Just before I finish, I’d just like to say that I, as the chair of this board, the Ngarimu
board, was very honoured to host the awards ceremony last week in Gisborne where we
presented about 13 awards to quite brilliant young Māori achievers. It was an absolutely
fantastic day, and I know that it means so much to them and their families to be carrying
that legacy with them. It’s incredible mana for them and the day couldn’t have gone
better, and I’d like to say a big shout -out to the board, who put on an incredibly good
awards ceremony.
And with that, Madam Speaker, I commend the Regulatory System s (Education)
Amendment Bill to the House.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The question is that the motion be
agreed to.

items.speaker: Hon JAN TINETTI
items.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I’m delighted to take a
very short call on the Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill. As the Minister
has pointed out, this bill has a number of changes to several Acts, and it really is one of
those omnibus bills that tidies up some issues that have been seen and found within the
legislation. It has made amendments to the Ngarimu VC and 28 th (Māori) Battalion
Memorial Scholarship Fund Act 1945, amendments to the Pacific Education Foundation
Act 1972, amendments to regulations of the Children’s (Requirements for Safety Checks
of Children’s Workers) Regulations 2015, and the Health and Safety at Work (General Risk
and Workplace Management) Regulations 2016.
Can I thank very much the work of the Education and Workforce Committee at the
time in the last Parliament, who took this work through. It’s actually nearly a year to the
day that the first reading of this bill occurred. It was 29 March when we had the first
reading. So it’s been a wee bit of time, even though there were only nine written
submissions and only three oral submissions for this particular bill.
As the Minister has quite rightly pointed out, most of the submissions were in favour
of the bill. In fa ct, some of those that were against the bill gave no reason why they
were against it. It was just a flat: “We don’t agree with this bill.” So most of the
submissions that came in were very fulsome in favour of the bill itself. As the Minister
has pointed out, the select committee had very minor changes that came back that tidied
it up somewhat, that made it a bit more of a bill that people could see as usable and
understanding of that bill.
The one thing I will say is that when the first reading did occur, almost a year ago,
the then Opposition members were quite scathing of this bill and didn’t seem to think
that it did much at all. I’m sure they understand now, when they’re on the other side,
that sometimes there are pieces of legislation that do make the legislation better. And it
doesn’t matter what they see as only minor changes to it, it is important to the people
for whom this legislation allows them to operate. And that’s exactly why these changes
have been made.
So I did say that I was going to take a very short call on this. I think that the bill is a
very good bill and I have no hesitation in commending it to the House.
2546 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024

items.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
items.text: I want to, first of all, echo what my predecessor
also said in terms of the different elements of this particular bill, the Regulatory Systems
(Education) Amendment Bill, and the fact that it’s an omnibus bill that looks at various
components. Also, I was not around when this bill was going through first reading nor
select committee, but upon again reading the notes to, and the Hansard of, the first
reading, I am glad to see that Minister Stanford is now in support of this bill. Particularly,
I am delighted to hear that she said the “wonderful and amazing and talented young
Māori” that she has met as part of the award ceremony. I’m hoping that this will change
her mind from the stance that she took in the first reading, that this is no t going to help
the achievement and the root cause of some of Māori and Pasifika performance, as we
have seen in the first reading.
So, in terms of this particular bill, a couple of things I would like to bring up as well,
particularly around the Ngarimu scholarships—and just to again highlight the fact that the
Ngarimu scholarships are designed to inspire, reward, and support Māori achievements and
their success in education. Ceremonies include doctoral, masters, undergraduate as well as
vocational education and training, which is absolutely fantastic to see that it cuts across all
levels of tertiary education, and also in the scholarships aimed to support the opportunities
for Māori students to reach their full potential by reducing some of the financial barriers to
study and/or training—again, fantastic to see.
In terms of the Pacific Education Foundation Act 1972, when we’re looking at that
particular thing—and again, please indulge me as I kind of go into some of these in a little
bit more depth —the gene ral purpose of the foundation should be to promote and
encourage the better education of Pacific people and to provide financial assistance for
that purpose. And for that we the Green Party agree that the omnibus bill and also the
results and the responses from the select committee report have achieved that.
A couple of additional things that I would like to point out that are particularly
noteworthy in this particular case as we are looking at things around Māori and Pasifika
student performance and also achievement are: number one, to look at the fact that the
authority expenditure in this case for the Pacific Education Foundation Act has increased
from $500 to $10,000 in reflection of the inflation, but also, most importantly, in reflection
to the cost of our education. I think I would like to take this opportunity to remind people
again that in these cases they shouldn’t have to take foundations and funding, that education
should be a public good and it should be free for all students.
The authority for unspecified expenditure in this case particularly was used for making
grants for uniforms and other equipment to Pacific learners and their families. Again, I
would like to point people to the recent investigation by the University of Otago around
the cost of new uniforms, which can range, on average, from $80 to over $1,200 per single
student. I am an educator, after all, and I know the kind of financial burden it places on
the students and their whānau.
There are also several steps that I think the New Zealand Government needs to take to
actually alleviate some of this when it comes to school uniforms, including making subsidies
for uniform costs more accessible and less bureaucratic, and the Government should legislate
this particular State funding for school uniforms for high-needs students.
The other angle to look at in this particular bill, which I think we hear in this House
repeatedly, is that the independence of Māori and Pasifika funding sources in this case is
absolutely crucial—on their funding sources that are determined by Māori and/or Pasifika
for Māori and Pasifika. In this particular case, I would like to highlight the Ministry of
Education submission, which is that this particular move is informed by wider
engagement and discussions with Pacific communities through the Ministry of Education
and, most importantly, the Ministry for Pacific Peoples from 2018 to 2023.
27 Mar 2024 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 2547
So, with all of that in mind, again, the Green Party is in support of this particular bill.
And, most importantly, we are in suppor t of the fact that we are looking at better
opportunities for our Māori and Pasifika students, as well as their families, in order to get
the best educational outcome. Thank you.

items.speaker: LAURA TRASK
items.text: Thank you. I stand in support of the Regulatory Systems
(Education) Amendment Bill. This is, essentially, an omnibus bill, and it’s essential that
we have our education regulatory systems fit for purpose.  So we definitely stand in
support of this.
I acknowledge that they’re just minor changes, especially to the 28 th Māori Battalion
to preserve its mana into the future. Hardly any members of the battalion are still alive
today, so this update in the legislation will ensure that Māori soldiers or veterans are
represented on the board for the future.
In relation to the Pacific Education Foundation, this bill will expand the list of Pacific
people to encompass the true representation of who Pacific people are today here in New
Zealand and who may now benefit. It updates the board’s constitution and expenditure, which
hasn’t actually been updated since 1972. So we feel that is very fair to do so.
When it comes to the amendments to the Health and Safety at Work Act, for the
regulations to ensure that police vets and risk assessments are undertaken for workers at
limited-attendance childcare centres before they begin work, we feel that this is very fair.
It will create consistency and will bring it in line with other children’s workers’
requirements. And that goes for the same thing around the safety checks. We think that
it’s very fair that the 18+ card is an acceptable form of identity, with the Kiwi Access
card as well, to reflect the name change that has occurred.
So a really short call, but, in essence, we support this bill, and I commend it to the
House. Thank you.

items.speaker: TANYA UNKOVICH
items.text: One of the things I’m enjoying about being a new
parliamentarian is learning about all of these laws and pieces of  legislation, many that
I’ve never heard about. I’m very pleased to be speaking on this, because this is one that
has educated me quite a lot. I’ve made some really great notes, which I’m going to share,
because I feel that is something that will not only reinforce the value of this legislation
but it will also enable me to remember it a bit more as I’m explaining it to others, because
I really do like to share with everyone what I do when I’m in the House.
New Zealand First is going to support the Regulato ry Systems (Education)
Amendment Bill—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Duncan Webb
items.text: Well, you are in Government.

items.speaker: TANYA UNKOVICH
items.text: Oh, did I hear a heckle over there? No, not yet. No, not a
heckle.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Do you want me to heckle you?

items.speaker: TANYA UNKOVICH
items.text: No, I don’t need any heckling. No, just be kind.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Great job! Great job!

items.speaker: TANYA UNKOVICH
items.text: Oh dear, heckling from behind. That’s something I didn’t
expect, Madam Speaker.
This bill addresses key regulatory frameworks within the education sector, aiming to
streamline processes and improve governance structures. Now, the bill seeks to enhance
the effectiveness of existing legislation and also to better serve the needs of students,
educators, and educational institutions.
Now, this bill makes changes this way: it amends the Pacific Education Foundation
Act 1972 by updating things such as eligibility criteria and also fostering greater
education and opportunities. The other bill that is amended is the Ngarimu VC and 28 th
(Māori) Battalion Memorial Scholarship Act 1945, also known as the Ngarimu Act. This
2548 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
ensures proper recognition and support for veterans and their contributions, and it’s one
way to ensure that their legacy remains as well, which is incredibly important.
This bill also strengthens safety protocols by updating regulations governing safety
checks for childcare workers. Now, everyone wants to ensure that their children are safe,
so this is a very important part of the bill. T his will ensure that there are heightened
standards, and also it will give piece of mind for parents and guardians. Now, these
targeted changes aim to address specific needs within the education sector, promoting
efficiency for all involved. To be a little bit more specific, the bill will amend the Health
and Safety at Work (General Risk and Workplace Management) Regulations 2016 —
that’s another thing I’ve had to learn as a new parliamentarian: to be able to say these
long names. This is done to ensure a req uirement to ensure that there is a police vet and
to conduct a risk assessment for any workers at a limited attendance childcare centre. This
will be done before they commence work—it is an extra precaution.
The other thing that this bill amends is the Children’s (Requirements for Safety Checks
of Children’s Workers) Regulations 2015 to include an additional reference to Kiwi
access cards, reflecting the name change of the 18-plus card.
So how does New Zealand First feel about this? Well, New Zealand First,  as a party,
we’re very committed to equitable and efficient processes and regulations.

items.speaker: Hon Rachel Brooking
items.text: Good to hear!

items.speaker: TANYA UNKOVICH
items.text: Yes, we are indeed. And we always support sustainable
development that enhance s the wellbeing of all New Zealanders. New Zealand First —
in our principles we prioritise collaboration, transparency, and accountability. That is
very important, especially when it comes to regulatory processes. So we ensure that
the policies are implement ed fairly and effectively. New Zealand First also believes
in the importance of access to education, for all New Zealanders, to ensure lifelong
learning opportunities for all.

items.speaker: Hon Scott Simpson
items.text: It’s in the coalition agreement too.

items.speaker: TANYA UNKOVICH
items.text: I believe that it is.

items.speaker: Hon Scott Simpson
items.text: Very good.

items.speaker: TANYA UNKOVICH
items.text: Yes, I believe it is. So why would we support this bill? Well,
New Zealand First —we believe that the proposed amendmen ts aim to enhance the
governance structures and they promote equitable access to education, particularly in the
rural areas and areas where people cannot get to easily. Also, it aligns with our policies
to improve access to education and support, as I’ve said—lifelong learning opportunities
for all. It reaffirms our commitment to building a quality public education system. That
is something that we really want —all of us in the coalition —and we want to prioritise
and ensure the wellbeing of all New Zealander s, which is why I will take the honour of
commending this bill to the House on behalf of New Zealand First.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: This next call is a split call. The first call
I’ve got—the Green Party is the second call, so I’ll take Dr Hamish Campbell.

items.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL
items.text: Thank you, Madam Speake r. It is a
great pleasure to rise to my feet to talk about the Regulatory Systems (Education)
Amendment Bill. It’s always a great topic when we come to talk about education. I think
education is the key to actually lifting the quality of life of all people , and it’s actually
something that was a key theme of my maiden statement. I think it’s very important,
education, so I’m very grateful that I’ve been given this opportunity to stand up and talk
about this amendment bill. A lot has been mentioned about thi s bill already. It’s talking
about maintaining the mana of the Māori Battalion and the legacy that they have forged
in the theatres of war; we much honour their sacrifices that we have freedom because
of their willingness to go to war.
27 Mar 2024 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 2549

items.speaker: Hon Scott Simpson
items.text: This Parliament is a war memorial as well.

items.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL
items.text: Yeah, actually, that’s a good point. This Parliament is a
war memorial, and we honour not just the Māori Battalion but all battalions that have
fought for our safety and our freedom.
But getting back to this bill, of course, the policy objective of this bill is to maintain the
effectiveness and efficiency of the regulatory systems established by the principal Acts that
it amends. And I appreciate that’s a very complicated way of saying that really what we
need to do is modernise this legislation that will stop the need for us to have to keep on
coming back and editing it or modifying it, amending it. We need to make sure that we
modernise it to make sure that we can keep that mana going forward.
Now, of course, there’s a whole range of things that this bill is going to do, but I think
probably we do have support right across the House, which is great. But I think it is great
that we can actually have scholarships which we can then give out to students, which can
give them encouragement to continue on into education so they can reach the aspirations
and dreams that they have. And, of course, it was just last night that, actually, we had
Rocket Lab here at Parl iament, and we think of the students that now can reach for the
stars. We can definitely encourage more students into STEM and actually help lift the
quality of life of all New Zealanders. But I do digress. I appreciate it is very much a
passion of mine that we do increase our scientific literacy of our students.
But this bill contains a range of minor and technical changes, as I say, aimed at
modernising and updating legislation. And, of course, we’ve talked about this
scholarship fund Act broadening the r ange, updating the definition of a Pacific person
who can benefit from this foundation. I think it’s very important that we acknowledge
that and can continue to elevate Pacific people in New Zealand. And, of course, we’ve
talked about changing the name of the ID card. Just once again, this shows that we need
to make sure that this is a modernised piece of legislation that will actually achieve what
we need it to do.
All parties have indicated their support for this bill, and I do believe there have been
some submissions through the select committee process—all in favour of this.

items.speaker: Hon Scott Simpson
items.text: With unanimity across the House.

items.speaker: Katie Nimon
items.text: Amazing.

items.speaker: Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL
items.text: It’s absolutely amazing. I think really the key messages
are we need to preserve the legacy and the mana of the 28 th Māori Battalion into the
future, we need to support the work of the Pacific Education Foundation, and we need
to ensure that the education regulatory systems are fit for purpose. And so, therefore, I
commend this bill to the House.
RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green): It’s a pleasure to rise in support of the
Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill. L ike other Opposition MPs, I’d like
to welcome the National Party speakers to the right side of supporting this piece of
legislation. I was looking at the Hansard record of the proceeding, and there were some
really interesting comments. But before I touch on some of those comments, I did want
to acknowledge the comments from my colleague Lawrence, who spoke earlier around
the importance of the independence of Māori and Pasifika funding sources and that those
are determined by Māori and Pasifika for their ow n communities, and also recognising
the importance of the Ngarimu scholarships and how they actually resource and inspire
Māori students and celebrate Māori achievement.
Which then takes me to the other points of the speakers from the first reading, because
I think this bill is actually about lifting achievement. It is about celebrating and supporting
Māori and Pasifika students. And yet in the first reading, there were several comments
from the Minister when she was in Opposition. She said, “Again, some noble intentions,
but misses the main point of the fact that our kids can’t do reading, writing, and math.”
2550 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
And she also said, “Nothing in this bill around achievement for Māori and Pasifika —
again, a missed opportunity.” For example, if we look at Penny Simmonds’ comments in
the first reading, she said, “Well, here we are again debating things with little to do with
education without hitting the real issues in the education sectors, but, however, we’ll have
another go at it.”
I think, to me, this just talks a bout the need for members to engage with bills in a
substantive way so that they actually look at the legislation in a way that is accurate. I don’t
know if it was submitters actually helping them to open their eyes or the advice that the
Minister received now that she’s in Government, but I’m really pleased to see that now
we’ve gotten to a place where we’re all supporting this bill. And this will be one of the few
times that I’ll be commending the ACT Party, because I was looking at the Hansard record
and I’m glad to see that they had at least a consistent position in this piece of legislation,
which is great. We do support people being consistent with their values, but when they’re
not, at least it’s good to see them come to the right side.
But coming bac k to the bill. This is a bill that we are happy to support because,
ultimately, what it does is it updates support that exists for Māori and Pacific students.
It continues ensuring that we celebrate that achievement. And, at the end of the day,
as Lawrence  said, there is more that we have to do to ensure that our education system
is fully accessible for all, but ultimately the things that we’re updating here and
maintaining the effectiveness and efficiency of the regulatory system still support that
broader participation of people in the education system. For those reasons, we
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: KATIE NIMON
items.text: I’m really pleased to be standing here to speak
to the Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill, and specifically to shed some light
on some context. On Friday, I was really privileged to join Minister Stanford in Gisborne
to attend the Ngarimu VC and 28th (Māori) Battalion Memorial Scholarships awards. For
those of you that don’t know, my electorate goes all the way up into Gisborne and
boundaries with that of my good friend and colleague Dana Kirkpatrick, to the southern
area of Gisborne District. So I was very privileged to be there and present with my friend
Dana, who knows so many of the community. It’s quite amazing to see her be greeted by
people with such joy. It was a real privilege to be there.
Erica did a fantastic job of acknowledging the very importance of, particularly, the 28th
Māori Battalion but also the Ngarimu VC scholarship awards and the history, and some
real history was shared on this particular scholarship fund while we were there. One of
the points—and there were so many points;  the whole ceremony was five hours, in the
glorious Gisborne sunshine, might I add. The history was that there was money put aside
in recognition of Ngarimu after his life was lost in the war, to acknowledge the
descendants of his family. I believe that ab out £7,500 was raised by parliamentarians at
the time in support. And with inflation, I think you could calculate it, it would be in the
millions in terms of what money was raised. As that has gone on over time, it has raised
a significant amount, so we’ve actually been able to contribute to the careers of the most
incredible, bright, young Māori people.
I just make a point as to why some of these changes in this bill are so important. One
young gentleman, Heremia McGarvey, I met at Lake Waikaremoana earli er this year
when I was with Minister Potaka —[Interruption] Yes, a fantastic Minister. We were
opening the Lake Waikaremoana track with Tūhoe iwi. Heremia is part of that iwi, and
I met him there. I thought, “What an impressive young man. He’s going to go a really
long way.” I have to say it was one of the most proud moments when I sat down in the
audience at the awards on Friday to see Heremia McGarvey’s name in the programme,
receiving a scholarship. He is studying law in Wellington, and I thought, “My go sh, he
really is an impressive young man.”
27 Mar 2024 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 2551
This award recognises men like him and some of the other men and women who receive
these scholarships. They were not just undergraduates. There were also those with a
doctorate, a Master’s, vocational education, and there were some incredible video
acknowledgments made. One was to the head girl of Rangitoto College, which the Minister
acknowledged herself, being a former student of Rangitoto College as well.
The point here in this bill is the change that is necess ary to be made, which is to
modernise the language so that we can protect organisations like this. The descendants are
very important to this, and it was hosted at C Company Memorial House. But it’s important
that the fund is administered and acknowledged to be in the right place. The other thing to
add—and we were very privileged to have Willie Apiata VC in our presence. It was an
incredible thing, I’ve got to say. One of the highlights of my day was meeting Willie Apiata,
a true hero—and, yes, he is tall. He spoke off the cuff. He didn’t know he was meant to be
speaking and he spoke off the cuff to his experiences and why this scholarship award is so
important. He made the point so perfectly himself that you’ve got to keep this going so that
those that receive it and those that go on to receive it understand how important it is and
what it means to the future of these young people —and, actually, they are not all young
people. Some are incredibly successful people in their 50s and 60s who have led incredible
lives and continue to study and contribute.
I’ve made acknowledgment of the board members and so one of the points in this bill
is about the board members of the Ngarimu VC scholarship and the scholarship fund Act.
Of course, we have representatives from Māori electorates, many of whom were there on
the day. I acknowledge my colleague Cushla Tangaere -Manuel, who is the member for
Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and was there representing her electorate. I think the point is that we’ve
got our Minister of Education, our Māo ri electorate MPs, and we have also got
representatives from the various companies within 28 th Māori Battalion. But to have a
new Māori representative position on the board, this is fundamental.
Just to draw your attention to it, there is on the board som eone that has served or is
currently serving in the New Zealand Defence Force. Now, that might be one Willie
Apiata VC. Now, I’m not going to do the Governor -General’s job and decide who it is
that’s going to take that position. But it felt quite interesting to me, sitting in the audience
and wondering why it was that he wasn’t on the board. He was such a significant part of
that organisation. He was there representing, but it’s because there is not a provisional
place for him on the board. Now, this amendment would allow that. Now, as I say, that’s
not to say that he necessarily will take that board position, but for this amendment to
create a position for him, I think, is something that will take this bill a really long way.
So, look, I say that that parti cular aspect of the bill is really important to me, and I say
I have experience with it —just to see the importance of what happens when you really
continue the legacy of something so fundamental to our country.
There is something to point out on the next aspect—and, obviously, this is a three-part
bill. A lot of people have referred to it as an omnibus bill. It does cover a lot of points,
but the next aspect is the Pacific Education Foundation. This is something really
interesting, and I’ve made a couple of  points here. Under the Pacific Education
Foundation, the amount that was meant for each financial year hasn’t been changed since
1972. My good friend and colleague Hamish Campbell made the point of modernising
this bill so we don’t have to keep changing it. What we’re doing here is allowing ourselves
to have this information change with time without having to constantly go back in and
make further changes.
Another point to make is about the “Aotearoa Pacific person”, a person who is living
in New Zealand, who is granted a permanent residence but is from a Pacific nation. Now,
I think this is really interesting to acknowledge. We’ve got an upcoming trip, a delegation,
to the Pacific Islands. Actually, it’s a Speaker’s delegation, and one of the countries tha t
2552 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
we are visiting is Niue. There’s a really interesting background on Niue: 1,950 people
live in Niue but more of them live in New Zealand. It’s important for us to acknowledge
those people under this programme.
I hear members opposite scoffing at this, but, actually, this was their bill, and had this
bill gone through under their time, I have no doubt they would speaking to all these points
in such depth. Now, all of a sudden it doesn’t sound as important to them as it did when
this bill was under their watch.
There are some really fantastic aspects to this bill, and I think that it’s important that I
highlight these. Unfortunately, some of these things are really necessary for us to change
and one of the points that I’ve got here is about the childcare centres. I am actually—and
it’s amazing that it’s taken me this long to bring it up —the chair of the Education and
Workforce Committee, and just recently we heard from the Associate Minister of
Education who’s responsible for early childcare education centres. What’s been identified
during his time as the Minister is that for some of these childcare centres that are attached
to, perhaps, gyms, for example, or malls, actually it hasn’t been a requirement for these
people to have police vetting. And so it’s real ly important. Some of the interesting
information in this bill is that employers—although they’re already required to police vet,
it’s not before they start employment.
I know from my experience managing a bus company that you have to vet all of your
staff. It is a fundamental part, but, actually, they need multiple police vets. If you were a
firefighter and you were a bus driver, you need to have two checks. It doesn’t matter that
you don’t need to necessarily go across both of those. And so when you start  in one of
these roles, it’s so fundamental that you are checked by police. My good friend and
colleague Carl Bates, known in Whanganui as the “everywhere man”, has two young
children in early childhood education, and an example for him would be knowing th at if
he were to take his children, when he was going to the gym, to a childcare centre, they
would have the same health and safety expectations and that his children would be safe
and with people who are fit and proper. Just to summarise the points we’ve got here, there
are three key aspects to this bill, and I think it’s really good.

items.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
items.text: Thank you very much for the call, Madam Speaker.
I didn’t think I was going to get an opportunity, such was the passion of the chair of the
Education and Workforce Committee, Katie Nimon, on matters relating, somewhat,
adjunctly, tangentially to the subject matter of this bill.
But this is a good bill and I was very pleased to be on the select committee when we
considered this bill, and I want to acknowledge—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Oh, were you the chair, then?

items.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
items.text: Yeah, I was actually the chair then, and I j ust want to
acknowledge the Minister at the time, Jan Tinetti, who brought this bill to the House, and
also acknowledge the current Minister, who was actually on the committee when we
considered it, as well. So it’s a very interesting bill.
One of the things that I have learnt being in Parliament is that this particular bill is an
omnibus bill. It does lots of things that might be considered minor to some people but, as
members have elucidated in their speeches, some are very significant things to particular
groups, including the 28 th (Māori) Battalion Memorial Scholarship Fund. So there are
some very important things in here.
I won’t go, as other members have, through every aspect of this bill, but two aspects
that I wanted to highlight are, firstly, the regulatory changes in relation to early childhood
education. It is really important to have good, solid safety regulations in  early childhood
education—perhaps one of the most important areas that we regulate in New Zealand. In
education, some of the most important regulations are in that early childhood space. The
reason that those are so important is because they help to keep some of the most
27 Mar 2024 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 2553
vulnerable people in our society safe. When we take our children to childcare centres, as
many in this House have done in the past, do currently do, or will do in the future, we
need to be absolutely certain that all of the checks and balances are in place to ensure the
safety of those children.
It’s been heartening to see the change of tone from members opposite in relation to these
regulatory matters. We have heard a lot of criticism about regulations in early childhood
education recently from members of the coalition Government. I would just like to emphasise
at this point that this shows how important regulations are. Of course people should go
through a police check when they are looking after your children, even if it’s for a short period
of time in a mall or a gym or other such location. So it just shows you that when we talk about
regulations, some of them can be incredibly important.
I want to commend the former Minister Jan Tinetti for bringing this bill to the House.
I want to commend the committee for considering it, as we did very carefully. We looked
at a lot of the definition words very carefully, we heard from representatives from the 28th
Māori Battalion, we made sure that we took this bill—although it’s not a bill that’s going
to revolutionarily change the country, we took it really seriously, and we did, I feel, bring
back a few changes. But also, having gone through that scrutiny process, which is so
important, we were assured that this bill does what it says on the tin.
So the only thing I just wanted to lastly talk about, which hasn’t been mentioned,
is that this is a very unusual bill in that it has a picture of an emblem as part of the
bill, which is 28 th Māori Battalion and a picture of that in Schedule 1. I just want to
draw the House’s attention to that, because it is quite unusual to see a pictorial element
of a particular piece of legislation in the bill, and very beautiful and full of history. So
I just want to acknowledge all those, as other people in the House have , who served
in the Māori Battalion, and those who continue to focus on the Māori Battalion’s
legacy as this bill does. I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: CARL BATES
items.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker, and thank
you for giving me the opportunity this evening to speak on the Regulatory Systems
(Education) Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: An important bill.

items.speaker: CARL BATES
items.text: It is an important bill, and it reminded me, actually, my wonderful
colleague the MP down there in Christchurch, Hamish Campbell—

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: Doctor.

items.speaker: CARL BATES
items.text: Dr Hamish Campbell —thank you—Dr Hamish Campbell speaking
about maiden speeches, and it reminded me of something that I said in my maiden speech:
that this House must make choices about what the role of Government is and what it is
not. We cannot and should not do everything, nor attempt to solve every problem. A nd
it’s bills like this that make sure our legislation is clear about what the Government will

That brings me to my colleagues on the  Education and Workforce Committee. I just
have to acknowledge the great mahi of our chairwoman, Katie Nimon —her excellent
speech just before where she traversed this bill, I think, very fully—and I acknowledge her
recognition of those members who have families and have children and how a bill like this
will just fix that little challenge that there is when it comes to childcare. But I’ll come back
to that, colleagues, a little later in my opportunity to share this evening.
I also want to acknowledge the gr eat member for the Wairarapa, great new member,
outstanding member, one of my rural and provincial colleagues, Madam Speaker, as are
2554 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
you, from one of the strong national parks of the country. And, Mike, it’s been great
learning from you on the Education and Workforce Committee. You always have questions
that really do hone in on the challenge that we’re identifying. And, of course, to Grant
“McNational”, I’m looking forward to your contribution on this bill this evening.
I also want to acknowledge Minister Erica Stanford, Minister of Education and chair
of the Ngarimu Trust. I think the opportunity that Katie Nimon and Dana Kirkpatrick had

Napier and of East Coast, to get to an event such as that and ensure that those 12 —am I
correct? Twelve? Thirteen?

items.speaker: Katie Nimon
items.text: Twelve.

items.speaker: CARL BATES
items.text: Twelve recipients on the day —yep, 12 or thereabouts —were well
recognised by the local members.
I also touched briefly in my maiden speech on a business that I’d been involved in
founding, and that happened to be in the space of creating boards and appointing boards.
So, with the amendment in this bill this evening, around the addition of the role of t he
Governor-General in appointing an additional member to the trust board of Māori
descent, it just takes me back to that time. I spent 16 years, in fact, being involved in
appointing boards here in New Zealand and around the world.
The role of having div ersity in the boardroom is really important, particularly when
it relates to the history and the reason for existence of the trust of the organisation, and
I think it’s a great step this evening that we are ensuring that opportunity to have the
appointment to this trust of someone of Māori descent to carry on that legacy of the
28th Māori Battalion. It is really important to ensure that the right individuals receive
these scholarships.
In fact, late last year, I suppose, as part of the “Mr Everywhere” —thank you, Katie
Nimon, that you referred to before —I happened to be in Stratford and I attended the air
cadets’ final parade for the year. It was the first time a local member of Parliamen t had
attended their final parade in Stratford in a number of years. In fact, it was long ago; they
couldn’t remember the last time a local member of Parliament had attended their final
parade. But it makes me wonder whether one of those young men or women  could be a

I want to come to the third part of this bill, which is around the addition of the police-
vetting amendment. The amendment is to ensure that not only do all childcare workers in

items.speaker: Hon PEENI HENARE
items.text: Kia ora, Madam Speaker, and thank you for
the opportunity to speak on this particular bill. I’m excited, as a former board member
of the Ngarimu VC trust—

items.speaker: Arena Williams
items.text: And recipient.

items.speaker: Hon PEENI HENARE
items.text: —and recipient—and also sitting next to a recipient —and
also the grandson of the final commander of the 28th Māori Battalion. It truly is an honour

And it was seen, actually at the time under the leadership of the Hon Hekia Parata and

items.speaker: GRANT McCALLUM
items.text: It’s with a great privilege I rise to
speak on this bill, the Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill. And I’d, again,
like to acknowledge the great work of the Education and Workforce Committee.
I’d like to acknowledge the work of the current select committee, where we have our
great chair, Katie Nimon. The MP for Napier does great work. She even manages to talk
about buses in a speech like this, which I thought was quite incredible. Then there is the
“everywhere man”, our deputy chair, Carl Bates, from Whanganui. He has to tell me he’s
everywhere, but he’s everywhere but here right now. And the n there is the great MP for
Wairarapa, Mike Butterick —a man who does actually go everywhere. He works really
hard for his people, and I would like to acknowledge him. And the other member of the
committee on our side of the House is Dr Parmjeet Parmar, a list MP for ACT. It’s great
to have her on the committee as well.
Look, I think it’s important, with this bill —I thought I’d start off, because the Māori
Battalion actually has a very significant part to play in our history. I think it’s really
important. So what the bill is doing is really establishing and recognising that —helping
recognise that and the importance and the history of that. And as was acknowledged by
the previous speaker, this Chamber recognises a lot of the battles that the Māori Battalion
fought in. For example, we have El Alamein up behind us, Cassino along there. These
were great battles. And the members of the Māori Battalion really fought with pride and
did their people and our country proud.
In fact, I’ve got a few little notes here about the history of the Māori Battalion. It was
formed in October 1939. The Government agreed to establish an all -Māori unit, and
they called it the 28 th Māori Battalion. And Māori were eager to prove their equality
with their Pākehā comrades as warriors and  to earn the full benefits and privileges of
citizenship, which seems ironic given some of the discussions we have today. Even in
27 Mar 2024 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 2559
1939, the Māori sense of being accepted as equals with the New Zealanders was
marginal, which seems quite incredible.
The Māor i Battalion was organised on tribal lines under tribal leaders. Overall
command initially went to George Dittmer, a Pākehā professional soldier and First World
War veteran. At first, there was some resentment towards a European commander, but
this was rapi dly overcome by Dittmer’s professional competence and strict discipline.
Later in the war, the battalion was commanded by a number of Māori officers, including
lieutenant colonels Tiwi Love, Fred Baker, Charles Bennett, Reta Keiha, Peter Awatere,
and Sir J ames Hēnare. I think it’s a privilege to have you in the House here today, sir.
Thank you.
The battalion trained for three months at the Palmerston North Showgrounds. And
on 1 May 1940, approximately 780 members of the Māori Battalion left for Egypt as
part of the 2nd New Zealand Expeditionary Force, second echelon. It would be followed
by 12 contingents of reinforcements and remain on active service for almost six years.
The battalion was diverted to the United Kingdom for the rest of 1940 to help defend
southern England.
And then into the battles. But actually there were battles in Greece —also up here —
Crete, and North Africa. In 1941, the battalion departed from England for North Africa.
From Egypt, it embarked on its baptism of fire: the defence of Greece. After its first battle
at Olympus Pass, the battalion made an exhausting withdrawal, evacuating to the island
of Crete. In the Battle of Crete, the Māori soldiers developed a reputation as feared
opponents in close quarters combat, and it was a reputation that continued to follow them
through the war.
The battalion fought through the North Africa campaigns of 1941 to 1943. It was
involved in taking Sollum and Gazala in Libya, the breakout of Minqar Qaim in Egypt,
and the Battle of El Alamein—a truly legendary battle. Against great odds, it captured the
key features of Tebaga Gap and Takrouna Pinnacle in Tunisa. Second Lieutenant Moana-
Nui-a-Kiwa Ngarimu was posthumously rewarded the Victoria Cross for his courage at
Tebaga Gap. The battalion is one of the reasons we are here today. The battalion’s hard
fighting was reflected in its casualty rate: 270 dead and 815 wounded. And every Anzac
Day, as we acknowledge the sacrifices of all the soldiers that fought in the various wars,
it’s those sorts of stats that really hit home. And once again, as we hit Anzac Day, we will
once again be remembering those battles and the sacrifices.
Of its seven commanders during this period, two were killed and three were
wounded. Initially, between 1943 and 1945, they fought in two battles in Italy, and the
battles were sobering. Its attack on Orsogna in December 1943 was rebuffed, with more
than 50 casualties. But it was at Casino where two of its company sustained horrendous
casualties during a failed attack on the railway stat ion, in February 1944. Of the
200 men who started out, 128 were killed, wounded, or captured. The advance on
Florence came next, followed by fighting around Faenza in December, before the
battalion took part in the final race to Trieste.
With the exception of 270 men who were deployed to Japan as part of the divisionary
cavalry regiment, the battalion returned to New Zealand in January 1946. Throughout the
war, they had 15,744 people who volunteered. Now, that’s something you have to
remember: it was an entirely voluntary force. While a lot of non-Māori were conscripted
to fight, the Māori volunteered, which I think is something we always must remember.
And they performed with distinction, both at home and abroad. The total Māori
population at the time was j ust under 100,000. More than 3,600 men, all volunteers,
served with the Māori Battalion. The battalion suffered 2,628 casualties: 649 of them
were killed, 1,712 were wounded, and 267 were taken prisoner or were missing. That’s
almost 50 percent more than the New Zealand average, which just showed the quality and
2560 Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill 27 Mar 2024
the fighting spirit of the men involved. The unit received 99 honours and awards —the
highest number among New Zealand infantry battalions.
When you hear the history, you can actually go and now visi t a great display —I’ll
just bring this one up, so I can get this right too. There is a really great display up at
Waitangi, and the Te Rau Aroha Museum. I commend you all, this Easter, to travel over
the Brynderwyn Hills up to Waitangi —to go and visit and see this great display. It’s
divided into three galleries and it’s really worth going to see —it’s very emotional and
I commend it to you.

items.text: I’ve seen it.

items.speaker: GRANT McCALLUM
items.text: Thank you, Katie; I appreciate those comment s. I’m just
recently in the process of being admitted on to the Waitangi National Trust, and the Hon
Peeni Henare is a current member of that trust, and, of course, Sir James Henare was one
of the last commanders of the Māori Battalion. So it’s an honour to be part of that and to
be part, a little bit, of actually helping to bring that history to the people of New Zealand
and to the people of the North, given the sacrifices all made.
So I really look forward to welcoming you all up there over Easter. I thin k
commending this bill to the House is a really important thing to do, because of the history
of all involved. So I commend the bill to the House. Thank you.
